01

Overview

Valueattics Re is India's first private reinsurance company, anchored by Fairfax Financial Holdings. As a new entrant in a regulated, relationship-driven category, it needed a visual identity that could speak to insurers, brokers and regulators — and still feel like a young, agile company rather than a legacy institution.

I was entrusted with the visual branding and day-to-day design execution for the brand. I independently handled the work across its website, communications, campaigns and physical touchpoints, with mentorship from Asif, Art Director at Digit Insurance.

This is the project where I stopped designing individual creatives and started designing a system.

02

The design challenge

Create a visual language that holds three things at once.

Credible

For a regulated institution

Operating under IRDAI and sitting beside a global parent brand, where restraint reads as trust.

Contemporary

For a new-age reinsurer

Positioned on agility and innovation, so the identity could not look inherited or institutional.

Flexible

Across very different formats

From a compliance-heavy website to a festive sticker, without losing recognition.

The core tension: the same system had to carry a disclosure footer and a Diwali greeting.

03

Constraints I designed within

ConstraintDesign implication
Regulated financial categoryRestraint in layout; hierarchy and legibility over decoration
Backed by a global parentIdentity must read as independent, not derivative
B2B audience — insurers, brokers, regulatorsClarity and information density over visual persuasion
Lean team, live brand, continuous outputThe system had to be reusable, not re-invented per asset
Print + digital + fabric + screenAssets built to hold up at every reproduction quality

Principles I worked to: consistency builds recognition · one system, many moments · simple before decorative · every asset should be reproducible by someone else.

04

The visual system

I extended the brand's deep blue and warm yellow into a complete working system rather than a colour pair.

Logo system

Approved lockups in stacked and horizontal formats, each carrying the Fairfax endorsement line, with documented clear-space rules and permitted colour treatments across light and dark backgrounds — so the mark stays consistent no matter who applies it.

Primaries carry the brand; secondaries exist only to keep illustration and festive work from feeling flat — a deliberate limit so the identity stays recognisable when the palette expands.

Typography

Aa

Primary typeface

ParkinSans

Geometric, highly readable, confident without being formal. Headlines in Bold, SemiBold or Extra Bold; body in Regular. Substitutions are not permitted.

Iconography

Custom icons built on flat brand-colour fills only, bold minimal geometry, and consistent line weights and proportions. Each icon maps to a specific capability or value rather than being decorative.

Lockups & proof points

A set of reusable banner formats carrying the brand's proof points, designed in multiple colour inversions so teams could pick a variant instead of improvising one.

Motif & illustration

The wave. The wave from the logomark became the brand's connective pattern — lanyards, packaging, stationery, ID cards, presentation backgrounds. One graphic device doing recognition work across unrelated formats.

Flat vector illustration. Characters in brand colours, used to make dense reinsurance content approachable. The surfer-on-a-wave became the brand's shorthand for agility and now anchors the website hero and environmental graphics.

05

Website

I designed the Valueattics Re website to bring corporate information, products, leadership, values and the partnership story into one clear experience. It is live at valueattics.com.

Key decisions

  • Sequenced the page around trust, not features — who we are, who backs us, how we partner, what we cover, who leads us.
  • Turned the product range into a scannable component system — thirteen lines of business and four solution types rendered as consistent icon cards instead of paragraphs.
  • Used illustration to open, structure to close — an approachable hero, then increasingly factual layouts down to the regulatory footer.
  • Built typography, cards, icons and illustration as one language, so the site reads as a system rather than a set of sections.

06

One identity. Many moments.

The same visual system had to work for formal announcements and for celebratory, festive and employee-facing moments — without losing recognition.

This work is published on the brand's social and internal channels — including LinkedIn and Instagram — alongside emailers and employee communication. Designing for a live feed added its own constraint: each post has to hold up on its own in a scrolling context and still read as part of the same brand when seen in sequence.

The rule I held: the logo, palette and typography stay fixed; only the cultural layer changes. Festive work borrows warmth from the secondary palette and decorative motifs, but never negotiates the identity.

07

From screen to workplace

The brand extended into everyday physical items to create continuity between what people see online and what they hold in the office.

Designing for fabric, jute, matte board and screen meant testing the mark at very different fidelities — the wave pattern and single-colour logo variants came directly out of that requirement.

09

Reflection

What worked

Committing to a documented system early. Once the Look Book existed, every new request became an application rather than a fresh design problem — which is what made a lean setup sustainable.

What was hard

Holding consistency on a live brand. Real timelines, real stakeholders and continuous output create pressure to solve each asset locally; resisting that is the actual discipline.

What I'd improve

Formal usage rules for the illustration system, sized to match the rigour of the logo and icon guidelines, and defined motion behaviour for the wave motif on digital surfaces.

What I took from it

Managing this breadth of a live brand taught me to think past individual creatives and design for systems, consistency, scalability and long-term recognition.
